2010A16.goal: In $\triangle ABC$ with integer sides, the bisector $BD$ splits $AC$ into $AD=3$, $DC=8$. We want the smallest possible perimeter. The angle bisector theorem fixes the ratio $AB:BC$.

tools.name: Angle bisector theorem
tools.why: The bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides.

2010A16.approach: Write $AB=3k$, $BC=8k$, $AC=11$. Integer sides force $k$ to be an integer. Use the triangle inequalities to find the smallest valid $k$.

check.q: If $AB:BC=3:8$ with integer sides, which could they be?

2010A16.bridge: Use the bisector ratio and triangle inequalities.
2010A16.recognize: Angle bisectors with given segments: the bisector theorem gives side ratios; triangle inequalities pick the scale.

2010A17.goal: A $3\times3\times3$ cube has a $2\times2$ square tunnel drilled through the centre of each face pair (three tunnels). We want the remaining volume: $27$ minus the union of the tunnels.

tools.name: Inclusion–exclusion for volumes
tools.why: Add, subtract pairwise overlaps, add back the triple overlap.

tools.name: Tunnel overlaps
tools.fact: \text{any two tunnels share the central }2\times2\times2\text{ cube}

2010A17.approach: Each tunnel is $2\times2\times3=12$. Every pair, and all three together, overlap in the same central $2\times2\times2$ cube.
2010A17.bridge: Inclusion–exclusion on the three tunnels, then subtract from $27$.
solution: Each tunnel has volume $12$; every overlap is the central $2\times2\times2$ cube ($8$).
2010A17.shortcut: Each hole leaves a $\tfrac12$-inch border, so what remains is a frame: $8$ corner cubes of side $\tfrac12$ and $12$ edge bars $\tfrac12\times\tfrac12\times2$. Volume $8\cdot\tfrac18+12\cdot\tfrac12=7$.
2010A17.recognize: Drilled cubes: inclusion–exclusion on tunnels; overlaps are the central blocks.

2010A18.goal: Bernardo's digits come from $1$–$9$, Silvia's from $1$–$8$; each forms the largest number from three distinct digits. We want $P(\text{Bernardo}>\text{Silvia})$. Split on whether Bernardo picks $9$.

tools.name: Conditioning on the 9
tools.why: Choose the other two digits from eight.

tools.name: Symmetry when no 9
tools.why: Both then pick from $\{1..8\}$ the same way.

2010A18.approach: If Bernardo picks $9$, his number starts with $9$ and beats Silvia. Otherwise both choose three digits from $1$–$8$, identically distributed; use symmetry with ties.

steps.title: No 9
steps.explain: Both pick from $\binom83=56$ equally likely sets; ties have probability $\tfrac1{56}$. So $P(B>S)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{55}{56}=\tfrac{55}{112}$.

2010A18.bridge: Condition on Bernardo picking $9$, then use symmetry.
solution: With probability $\tfrac13$ Bernardo has a $9$ and wins.
2010A18.shortcut: Descending arrangement means each number corresponds to a $3$-element set; compare sets.
traps: Treating the numbers as ordered picks (permutations).
2010A18.recognize: Comparisons with a slight asymmetry: condition on the asymmetric part; the rest is symmetric.

2010A19.goal: An equiangular hexagon has sides alternating $1$ and $r$; triangle $ACE$ has $70\%$ of its area. We want the sum of possible $r$. Express both areas in terms of $r$.

tools.name: Equiangular hexagon as a cut triangle
tools.fact: \text{extend the sides of length }1\text{: big triangle of side }2r+1\text{ minus three triangles of side }r

2010A19.approach: $\triangle ACE$ is equilateral with side$^2=r^2+r+1$. The hexagon equals an equilateral triangle of side $2r+1$ with three corner triangles of side $r$ removed. Set the ratio to $0.7$ and use Vieta.

steps.title: Equation
steps.explain: $r^2+r+1=0.7(r^2+4r+1)$ gives $3r^2-18r+3=0$, i.e. $r^2-6r+1=0$. Both roots are positive; their sum is $6$.

check.q: What is the sum of the roots of $r^2-6r+1=0$?

2010A19.bridge: Write both areas in $r$, set the ratio, and add the roots with Vieta.
2010A19.shortcut: Vieta gives the sum without solving.
traps: Computing the hexagon area as six equilateral triangles (it is not regular).
2010A19.recognize: Equiangular hexagons: extend alternate sides to a big equilateral triangle and subtract corners.

2010A20.goal: A fly tours all $8$ corners of a unit cube in a closed loop of straight segments. We want the longest possible loop. Each segment is $1$, $\sqrt2$ or $\sqrt3$.

tools.name: Matching bound
tools.why: Each corner lies on exactly one space diagonal, and space diagonals in the loop cannot share a corner... each corner has only one, so at most $8/2=4$.

2010A20.approach: The loop has $8$ segments. Space diagonals pair up corners, so at most $4$ segments are $\sqrt3$; the rest are at most $\sqrt2$. Show $4\sqrt3+4\sqrt2$ is achievable.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.explain: $8$ segments; each corner has only one space diagonal and two segments of the loop touch it, so at most $4$ space diagonals. Bound: $4\sqrt3+4\sqrt2$.

check.q: How many space diagonals does a cube have?
check.why: One per pair of opposite corners.

steps.title: Achieve it
steps.explain: Alternate: space diagonal, then face diagonal. Example: $000\to111\to100\to011\to010\to101\to001\to110\to000$, which alternates $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt2$.

check.q: What is the distance from $(1,1,1)$ to $(1,0,0)$?

2010A20.bridge: Bound the number of space diagonals by $4$ and fill the rest with face diagonals.
solution: At most $4$ of the $8$ segments can be space diagonals ($\sqrt3$); the others are at most $\sqrt2$.
2010A20.shortcut: Space diagonals form a perfect matching of the corners.
traps: Assuming the fly must travel along edges.
2010A20.recognize: Longest tours through cube vertices: bound how often the longest segment can be used.

2010A21.goal: $x^3-ax^2+bx-2010$ has three positive integer roots. By Vieta, $a$ is their sum and $2010$ their product. We minimise the sum of three positive integers with product $2010$.

tools.name: Balance factors
tools.fact: \text{sums are smaller when factors are close}

2010A21.approach: $67$ is in one root. The other two roots multiply to $30$ (if the $67$-root is just $67$); keep them close: $5$ and $6$.

steps.title: Place 67
steps.explain: One root contains $67$. Making it exactly $67$ keeps it smallest; the other two multiply to $30$.

check.q: Which pair with product $30$ has the smallest sum?

2010A21.bridge: Use Vieta and split $2010$ into three balanced factors.
solution: $a$ is the sum of three positive integers with product $2010=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot67$.
2010A21.shortcut: The large prime dominates; balance the remaining factors.
2010A21.recognize: Roots with fixed product: minimise the sum by balancing factors (Vieta).

2010A22.goal: Eight points on a circle, all chords drawn, no three concurrent inside. We count triangles whose three vertices are all interior intersection points. Each such triangle comes from three chords that pairwise cross.

tools.name: Three pairwise-crossing chords
tools.why: Chords sharing an endpoint meet on the circle, not inside.

tools.name: Six points give one triangle
tools.fact: \text{the three "long" diagonals of the hexagon cross pairwise}
tools.why: Among the chords on $6$ points, only the three connecting opposite points all cross each other.

2010A22.approach: An interior triangle's sides lie on three chords that pairwise cross inside, so they use $6$ endpoints. Conversely, any $6$ points give exactly one such triple. Count $\binom86$.

steps.title: Triangles to 6-point sets
steps.explain: Each side of the triangle lies on a chord; the three chords cross pairwise inside, so their $6$ endpoints are distinct.

check.q: Can two chords that share an endpoint cross inside the circle?
check.why: They already meet at the shared endpoint.

steps.title: Count
steps.explain: For $6$ points labelled in order $1$–$6$, the chords $14$, $25$, $36$ cross pairwise; no other triple does. So the count is $\binom86=28$.

2010A22.bridge: Match interior triangles with sets of $6$ points.
solution: An interior triangle is formed by three chords crossing pairwise, using $6$ distinct points.
Each $6$-point set gives exactly one such triple (the "long diagonals").
2010A22.shortcut: Interior intersection points $\leftrightarrow\binom n4$; interior triangles $\leftrightarrow\binom n6$.
traps: Counting all triangles in the figure (many use circle points).
2010A22.recognize: Points and figures formed by chords of a circle in general position: count by choosing endpoint sets.

2010A23.goal: Box $k$ has $1$ red and $k$ white marbles. Isabella draws one from each box until red. $P(n)$ is the chance she stops at box $n$. We want the smallest $n$ with $P(n)<\tfrac1{2010}$. The product telescopes.

tools.name: Telescoping product
tools.why: Each numerator cancels the previous denominator.

tools.name: Stopping probability
tools.why: White from boxes $1$ to $n-1$, then red from box $n$ (probability $\tfrac1{n+1}$).

2010A23.approach: Compute $P(n)=\tfrac{1}{n(n+1)}$, then find the smallest $n$ with $n(n+1)>2010$.

steps.title: Formula
steps.explain: White from box $k$ has probability $\tfrac{k}{k+1}$. Product for $k<n$: $\tfrac1n$. Red from box $n$: $\tfrac1{n+1}$.

2010A23.bridge: Telescope the product to get $P(n)=\tfrac1{n(n+1)}$ and solve.

2010A24.goal: We want the last two nonzero digits of $90!$, i.e. $N=\tfrac{90!}{10^{21}}\bmod100$ (there are $21$ factors of $5$). Work mod $4$ and mod $25$ separately.

tools.name: Runs of four mod 25
tools.why: Expanding, the extra terms are multiples of $5m\cdot50$, which are multiples of $25$.

2010A24.approach: $N$ still has $86-21=65$ factors of $2$, so $N\equiv0\pmod4$. For mod $25$: $\tfrac{90!}{5^{21}}=(\text{product of non-multiples of }5\text{ up to }90)\times\tfrac{18!}{5^3}$. Use runs of four to evaluate each part, then divide by $2^{21}$.

steps.title: Non-multiples of 5 up to 90
steps.explain: They form $18$ runs of four, each $\equiv-1\pmod{25}$: product $(-1)^{18}=1$.

2010A24.bridge: Remove the $21$ tens; find the result mod $4$ and mod $25$, then combine.
2010A24.shortcut: The runs-of-four fact makes long factorial products mod $25$ quick.
2010A24.recognize: Last nonzero digits of factorials: strip the tens, then work mod $4$ and mod $25$.

2010A25.goal: Jim repeatedly subtracts the largest square. We want the smallest start giving a sequence of $8$ numbers (seven subtractions). Build the smallest starts backwards.

tools.name: Greedy step
tools.why: $s^2$ is the largest square at most $N$ exactly when $r<(s+1)^2-s^2$.

2010A25.approach: Let $f(k)$ be the smallest number needing $k$ subtractions. Then $f(k+1)=s^2+f(k)$ with the smallest $s$ satisfying $f(k)<2s+1$. Start from $f(1)=1$.
2010A25.bridge: Build the smallest starts backwards using $N=s^2+r$ with $r<2s+1$.
2010A25.shortcut: Each step needs $s\approx\tfrac{f(k)}{2}$, so values grow roughly like squares of halves.
traps: Using $s$ too small, so $s^2$ is not the largest square.
2010A25.recognize: Greedy processes: reverse them, choosing the smallest valid predecessor at each step.
